items.feedback: Right. What makes it an agent is the loop: the model picks an action, the program runs it, and the result comes back. A longer prompt or a bigger model only changes what a single call can do.
Right. The model only outputs a request that names check_calendar and gives the arguments. The program around it runs the tool. Hold on to that split, because your next answer blurs it.

You chose 'left to run longer, it will eventually fix the bug'. That is tempting, but the agent is getting the same failing result every step, so more steps add nothing new. It would just keep spending your budget. An agent needs a stopping condition, such as a step limit that ends the loop and reports back to a person. For a small model budget this matters a lot.

Your count of 4 is right: three tool requests plus the final answer. Your reason is off, though. You wrote that the model 'runs' each tool itself. It doesn't. Each call, the model only requests a tool, and the program runs it and sends the result back. Counting 'one call per input the model receives' (the question plus three results) gives the same 4 and keeps that split clear.

Right, and you gave both parts. The result goes back in as the model's next input, and the model uses it to decide its next step. The group-chat comparison works: the model only sees the result because it was added to the conversation.

The name does matter, so that is part of it. But the model relies on the whole description the program gives it: the tool's name, what it does, and the parameters it takes. A name alone can mislead. For example, check_calendar doesn't say whether it needs a machine, a date, or both. This is also why writing a clear description for each of your tools is a core design job.

summary: You have the loop down: what makes an agent, what the model outputs for a tool call, and what happens to a tool result. Two things to work on. First, an agent needs a stopping condition, because it will not necessarily get there by running longer (q3). Second, the model only requests tools and the program runs them (q4), and it chooses tools from their full descriptions, not just names (q6). Next step: write a description for check_calendar (purpose and parameters) and explain how the model would use it to decide between that tool and search_manuals.
